name: Chronic Disease Patient Education
description: A calm patient-education system with plain-language explanations, reassuring medical green, clear care-level guidance, practical habit tools, and predictable follow-up planning.
style_guide:
# Chronic Disease Patient Education

## Visual concept

This English-language style is designed for clinicians and health educators explaining chronic conditions, risk signs, daily management, and follow-up. It should feel calm, respectful, and practical rather than clinical or frightening: warm paper backgrounds reduce visual stress, medical green builds continuity, coral and amber distinguish care urgency, and plain-language diagrams turn abstract physiology into memorable actions. Every page should help a patient answer one question—what is happening, what should I notice, what can I do today, and when should I contact my care team.

## Canvas, grid, and safe area

- Use a fixed `1280 x 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Keep `64–76 px` safe margins. All medication, symptom, emergency, source, and contact information must remain comfortably inside the canvas.
- Use a 12-column grid with `18–22 px` gutters. Typical layouts are 6/6 promise split, 7/5 explainer-plus-myths, three equal care-level cards, four equal management cards, and 5/4/3 tool columns.
- Reserve a compact chapter line at the top with a short green rule, chapter number, title, and page count. Keep a quiet series label or source line at the bottom.
- Place the main headline high on the page and keep `24–36 px` before the explanatory sentence or main exhibit.
- Align cards, diagrams, safety panels, timelines, and resource lists to shared guides. Use `18–24 px` between modules and at least `14 px` internal padding around body copy.
- Keep every reading path obvious. Patients should not have to infer whether to read across, down, or by color.

## Color system

### Core colors

- Care paper: `#F5F0E7`. Use as the dominant canvas.
- Clinical green: `#4B8175`. Use for chapter lines, key terms, diagrams, routine guidance, and primary data.
- Deep care green: `#2F665A`. Use for resource panels, safety bands, selected KPI cards, and reverse text fields.
- Patient ink: `#253137`. Use for headlines, body text, card titles, and primary values.
- Clean white: `#FFFFFF`. Use for instructional cards, myth/fact rows, charts, and timelines.

### Supporting colors

- Gentle coral: `#CC7A5D`. Use for caution, myth labels, important transition words, and one supporting category.
- Safety amber: `#E8B83F`. Use for call-soon guidance, practical tips, and attention markers.
- Alert red: `#B94A42`. Use only for urgent action or emergency guidance.
- Soft mint: `#D7E5E0`. Use for routine labels, icon backgrounds, and inactive chart bars.
- Warm line: `#D8CEBD`. Use for borders, dividers, timeline rails, and chart grids.
- Body gray: `#617078`. Use for explanatory copy, metadata, and captions.

### Usage rules

- Care paper and Clinical green should dominate. Gentle coral and Safety amber provide hierarchy; Alert red is rare and strictly safety-related.
- Use one principal accent meaning per page and pair every color with a written label such as routine, call, or urgent.
- Keep warning panels readable without creating alarm. Use direct instructions, sufficient white space, and calm language.
- Do not use decorative gradients, neon colors, or blue-and-red hospital branding unless required by an established clinical identity.
- Never use color as the only way to distinguish risk or action.

## Typography

- Primary font: `Inter`, `Aptos`, or `Helvetica Neue`; fallback: `Arial, system-ui, sans-serif`.
- Use a regular sans serif for large reassuring statements and a bold weight for actions, symptoms, and key terms.
- Cover title: `64–84 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `0.98–1.08`; emphasize one condition or action phrase in Clinical green italic.
- Content headline: `42–58 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.02–1.12`.
- Chapter label: `11–14 px`, weight `700`, with `2–3 px` tracking, Clinical green.
- Section title: `24–32 px`, weight `500–650`.
- Card title: `20–26 px`, weight `500–650`.
- Body copy: `16–20 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.4–1.6`. Prefer short sentences and familiar words.
- Action label: `13–16 px`, weight `700–800`; make emergency actions visibly stronger than surrounding copy.
- Chart labels, notes, sources, and page numbers: `11–14 px`. Avoid footnotes that are too small for a patient-education setting.
- Use sentence case. Reserve uppercase for short chapter labels, levels, and safety tags.

## Layout and components

- Cards use Clean white with `1 px` Warm line borders, `10–14 px` corner radii, and no or extremely subtle shadow.
- Plain-language explainer diagrams use three large circular stages, simple familiar symbols, one-direction arrows, and a short takeaway band.
- Myth/fact rows use two balanced columns separated by a fine rule. Label the misconception and correction explicitly; do not imply blame.
- Care-level cards use a colored top rail, a written level tag, a short action-oriented title, no more than four signs, and a final What to do band.
- Management-pillar cards use one simple icon, a numbered label, one habit explanation, and a pale habit-anchor strip.
- KPI rows show one large value with a plain-language interpretation and the population or evidence context.
- Food diagrams use clear proportions and direct labels. Movement charts use a visible target line and daily labels.
- Tracking panels use Deep care green with high-contrast entries and a prominent frequency at the right.
- Follow-up timelines use a single horizontal rail, five or fewer visit markers, and plain-language descriptions of what happens at each visit.

## Charts and data

- Favor instructional diagrams, three-level action cards, proportion graphics, simple weekly bars, one-page tracking lists, and care timelines.
- Clinical green is the primary series; Soft mint shows below-target or inactive states; Amber indicates attention; Alert red indicates urgent action only.
- Direct-label every threshold, duration, frequency, unit, and target. Spell out abbreviations at first use.
- Keep charts focused on behavior or follow-up. Avoid dense lab dashboards, probability graphics, and unlabeled risk scores.
- Medical thresholds, treatment effects, medication instructions, and care intervals must be reviewed for the intended condition, population, and jurisdiction by a qualified clinician.
- Distinguish general education from personalized medical advice. Include the appropriate local emergency instruction and care-team contact path.
- Cite current authoritative clinical guidance near the relevant statement. Do not copy example diagnoses, dosages, symptoms, or schedules from preview imagery without verification.

## Page variations

- Cover: a calm 6/6 split with the title and presenter details on Care paper, then a Deep care green promise panel with one supportive statement and two compact program facts.
- Condition and misconceptions: a large plain-language mechanism diagram on the left and three myth/fact rows on the right.
- Symptoms, risks, and when to seek care: three equal routine, contact, and urgent cards with explicit action bands, followed by one full-width safety reminder.
- Treatment principles and daily management: four equal habit cards across the upper body and a row of realistic supporting measures below.
- Diet, movement, and tracking: a balanced-plate diagram, a simple seven-day activity chart, and one Deep care green health-log panel.
- Follow-up and trusted resources: a twelve-month care timeline across the left, recurring-care tasks below, and a high-contrast resource column on the right.

## Imagery and icons

- Prefer simple explanatory illustrations, familiar household or health symbols, accessible diagrams, and authentic clinical or daily-life photography when it adds understanding.
- Use one consistent icon style with rounded, friendly forms and direct labels. Icons support the words; they never replace a written instruction.
- If people appear, represent the intended patient population respectfully and obtain appropriate consent and licensing.
- Keep images free of fear-based anatomy, visible distress, needles, wounds, or dramatic emergency scenes unless medically necessary and appropriately contextualized.
- Do not use product branding or identifiable patient data as decorative evidence.

## Avoid

- Do not use fear, blame, shame, infantilizing language, or promises of cure.
- Do not present sample symptoms, thresholds, treatment effects, medication directions, or follow-up intervals as universal facts.
- Do not use decorative medical stock, glossy gradients, crowded dashboards, 3D anatomy, or dense paragraphs.
- Do not reduce body type, diet, adherence, disability, or disease control to moral judgment.
- Do not bury urgent actions, contraindications, uncertainty, or contact details in small print.
- Do not use unsupported wellness claims, invented citations, fake patient quotations, or unreviewed clinical statistics.
- Do not let visual simplicity remove essential nuance; add a clear clinician-reviewed note when guidance depends on individual circumstances.
